headline: Italy: budget amendments propose legal cannabis sales, home growing
dek: Two amendments to Italy's 2027 budget bill, published on 23 November, propose legal cannabis sales: one through a state monopoly, one with a 37% excise tax.
key_points: Italy's Chamber of Deputies Budget Committee published amendments on 23 November to the 2027 budget bill, C. 3174-bis, that would legalize adult-use cannabis.
Amendment 34.02, led by Marco Grimaldi, would extend Italy's state monopoly to cannabis and allow five female plants at home.
Amendment 34.01, from Riccardo Magi and Benedetto Della Vedova, would start licensed sales on 1 January 2028 with three home plants and a 37% excise tax.
Neither amendment has been approved, and both would need to survive committee and floor votes on the government's budget.
body: Two proposals to legalize adult-use cannabis in Italy have been tabled as amendments to the government's 2027 budget legislation. The texts were published on 23 November by the Budget Committee of the Chamber of Deputies, attached to bill C. 3174-bis, according to The Marijuana Herald, which linked to the committee's amendment file.

The two amendments take different routes to the same place. One would fold cannabis into Italy's existing state monopoly system, much like tobacco. The other would create a licensed market with a dedicated excise tax and a start date in 2028. Neither has been approved, and the Herald reported no vote on either.

Amendment 34.02 is sponsored by nine lawmakers led by Marco Grimaldi. It would extend Italy's state monopoly framework to the commercial cultivation, processing, import and sale of cannabis and products made from it, the Herald reported. Adults could grow up to five female plants for personal use and pass small quantities to others for immediate consumption.

Control would sit with two existing state bodies. The Customs and Monopolies Agency, known as ADM, would issue cultivation and retail licences and oversee processing. The Ministry of Economy and Finance would set production quantities, taxation, retail prices and how many outlets there are and where.

Amendment 34.01 comes from Riccardo Magi and Benedetto Della Vedova. It would legalize recreational sales from 1 January 2028 and allow up to three plants at home. Sales would carry a 37% excise tax, with the revenue used to cut taxes on employment and self-employment; medical cannabis products would be exempt. The text would ban advertising and sales to minors, require labels showing THC and CBD content, and set up product safety and supply-chain tracking rules, according to the Herald.
> Italy's two proposals split on one question that every legal market must answer: should the state sell cannabis, or tax those who do?

Set side by side, the differences are sharp. The monopoly plan allows more home growing, five plants against three, but gives the state control over volumes, prices and store numbers. The licensed plan has fewer plants but a defined tax, a fixed start date and explicit rules on advertising, labelling and tracking. In the monopoly model, prices and supply are policy decisions; in the licensed model, they are left largely to a regulated market with a heavy tax on top.

For investors and producers, the licensed model is the one that would create a recognisable commercial opening, with licences, a known tax rate and a start date. The monopoly model would be closer to a state procurement market, where suppliers sell to, or are licensed by, a single public buyer.

Italy's highest court has ruled that limited home cultivation can, in some circumstances, fall outside the criminal ban, the Herald noted. That has left personal growing in a grey zone decided case by case, and both amendments would replace it with a clear plant limit.

Italy's medical market is run largely by the state already. As we reported on 23 November, the government told the Chamber on 18 November that it has funding to double the greenhouses at the military pharmaceutical plant in Florence, aiming for at least 700 kilograms of medical flower a year by 2028, against health ministry estimates of about 2,400 kilograms of national demand in 2026. A monopoly-based adult-use market would extend that state-led model; a licensed one would break from it.

The Italian proposals arrive as other European countries test the boundaries of their own rules. In Germany, the association of cannabis-dispensing pharmacies proposed on 23 November a supervised pilot letting pharmacies sell to registered adults without a prescription, as we reported on 25 November. Across Europe, the debate is shifting from whether to allow adult use to how supply should be organised.

Watch the Budget Committee's voting on amendments to C. 3174-bis, where admissibility rulings and committee votes will decide whether either text survives. Watch whether the government signals any position on the amendments, and whether any of their elements, such as home growing limits, resurface as stand-alone bills if the budget route fails.
